newsitem.title: EGYPT: Frogmen retrieve dead from capsized Nile cruiser.
newsitem.headline: Frogmen retrieve dead from capsized Nile cruiser.

text.p: Egyptian frogmen and other rescue workers retrieved the bodies of three east European tourists from a capsized Nile cruiser on Friday and officials said they feared another 17 people had also drowned.
Eleven Czech and Slovak tourists and six Egyptians are still missing, believed trapped in the flooded cabins of the cruiser the Amira Jihan which capsized in a freak storm on Thursday afternoon.
The boat is lying on its side, half-submerged and grounded on a sand bank in the middle of the Nile off the village of Qalh al-Jabal, about 580 km (360 miles) south of Cairo.
More than 100 people -- about 63 tourists and 45 Egyptians -- survived the capsize and the tourists, mostly Czechs and Slovaks, have gone to the nearby tourist resort of Luxor.
Officials at the scene said they doubted any of the missing people would still be alive in the cabins after almost 24 hours, though some may have found pockets of air.
Frogmen continued to dive around the hull of the boat on Friday afternoon in the search for the other missing.
Officials at the scene named the confirmed dead as a Czech couple, Ian Biovsky and his wife Juka, and a Polish woman, Iren Szendziolorz, whose husband Teodor is among the survivors.
Ashraf Bennan, an Egyptian tour guide who was on the boat at the time, said Biovsky had celebrated his 50th birthday with a party on the morning of the accident.
Bennan said the boat suddenly listed some time between 3.30 and 4 p.m. on Thursday, at an hour when many of the tourists were resting in their cabins after lunch.
"I was in the restaurant on the lower deck talking to a friend of mine when I felt the boat lean," he told Reuters.
"I ran up quickly and the pressure of the water broke the windows behind me. We pulled as many people as we could out of the cabins but the only tools we had were ropes," he added.
"Another tour ship moored beside us and helped to take on some of the passengers," he said. Local people also came out to help with small boats.

Villagers in Qalh al-Jabal said the winds had been unusally strong on Thursday afternoon, strong enough to bend the palm trees along the Nile. The current is also in full spate these days because of heavy rains in Ethiopia this year.

Bennan and the Interior Ministry in Cairo said the boat was carrying 77 tourists and 51 Egyptians -- five tour guides and 46 crew. The ministry said all the tourists were either Czechs or Slovaks but Bennan said there were three Poles among them.
Before the three bodies were recovered, the Interior Ministry said the missing were nine Czech and five Slovak tourists and six Egyptian crew members.
Czech consul Vratislav Janda, who later left for Luxor, told Reuters: "The missing people are from the cabins that are under the water. Two of the survivors are badly injured, one with a broken leg."
The survivors spent the night in hospital in the town of Edfu and Janda said most of them moved on Friday morning to a hotel in the resort of Luxor.
"Of course they left the boat with just the clothes they were wearing. They don't have passports or any of their possessions," he added.
The cruiser was making the popular trip from Aswan to Luxor, passing by the Pharaonic temples of Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna.
It was the worst accident on such a cruiser for many years, though disasters with local ferries are more common.
Dozens of people drowned in September when an overloaded ferry capsized while bringing them home from a funeral. That accident took place further north, in the province of Minya.
